candidates.title: This wouldn’t have sounded possible a year ago, but it’s becoming much more reasonable now that you can get 10X output gains based on the latest in AI model and harness progress. The result is that teams within the same company are driving very different levels of output based on how they’ve adopted AI. This is a different phenomenon from other tech. Typically in the economy you think of technology adoption rates on a per firm basis, because the company generally adopts a relatively standardized approach to doing the new tech thing. Like “that company has gone digital or adopted the cloud”. So generally the uplift across teams is more or less the same across teams. AI is starting to look quite different. Even within the same company you can have a 10X delta between the lowest and highest adopters of AI and the impact they’re seeing. The teams that are able to actually figure out how to redesign their processes to best deploy agents in their workflows can see up to an order of magnitude jump in productivity depending on the job function. Right now this is heavily concentrated in coding, but more work will become coding adjacent so we can expect similar results elsewhere too. This is going to definitely lead to some wild dynamics within companies.

candidates.title: the predictions around the Jensen saga were a great demo of how little correlation there is between confidence and being right. it’s wild how many prominent VCs, analysts and experts spoke with complete confidence about how things would play out . some flip-flopped on their predictions within days - each time with the same confidence! our info ecosystem asymmetrically rewards certainty, speed and brashness… “I don’t know, let’s see how this plays out” just doesn’t get eyeballs. worth remembering with ALL “expert” commentary you consume - people often have far less certainty than their tone suggests. they just form a view, stake out a position and say it loudly. take everything with a sack of salt. this news cycle was also a good way to calibrate on the people who are consistently loud and wrong.

candidates.title: America can build the best frontier models and still lose the global AI race. Which is why Jensen’s return matters far beyond Nvidia. Governments around the world want sovereign AI: models they can run on their own soil, on their own infrastructure, under their own control. If American companies won’t meet that demand, Chinese companies will. Countries will start with Chinese models, then adopt Chinese infrastructure and chips. Having the smartest model won’t mean much if most of the world runs on someone else’s stack. We’ve seen a version of this play out with Huawei. China understood that supplying the world’s telecom infrastructure creates lasting strategic influence. Once a country builds its networks around your equipment, it also builds technical expertise, supplier relationships, and future investment around it. Replacing that equipment becomes expensive and disruptive (the US government is now trying to finance replacement operations but it’s been difficult). That’s why Jensen’s backing of the American open-model ecosystem is so important. Open models give startups the freedom to compete and give countries a reason to build on American technology. We need both frontier leadership and global adoption. Open models are essential to getting both. https://t.co/f34FKKbljl
